grammar.title: Grammatik
grammar.rule: Der Mann ist hier. Die Wäsche ist sauber. Das Zimmer ist kalt. Hier ist Jakob. Jakob ist nicht groß.
grammar.note_en:
A noun names a person, place or thing. German writes nouns with capitals. Learn each noun with its grammatical gender: masculine der Mann (“the man”), feminine die Mutter (“the mother”), neuter das Zimmer (“the room”). Gender belongs to the German word: a room is not biologically neuter. These are nominative forms: the forms used to name the subject, the person or thing the sentence is about. The definite article der/die/das roughly means “the”; the indefinite article ein/eine means “a/an”: ein Mann (“a man”), eine Woche (“a week”), ein Zimmer (“a room”). Masculine and neuter both use ein here. These tables show only encountered singular forms, not all German articles.

Sein is “to be”. A finite verb is a verb form tied to its subject: ich bin (“I am”), er/sie/es ist (“he/she/it is”). Ich bin Jakob Lauer means “I am Jakob Lauer”; Der Kolben ist leer means “The flask is empty”. An adjective describes something. After ist it has no added ending: Die Wäsche ist sauber (“The laundry is clean”). Pronouns stand for nouns: er for a masculine noun, sie for a feminine noun, es for a neuter noun. Thus Die Wäsche … Sie ist weiß means “The laundry … It is white”, not “she is white”.

In a normal statement the finite verb occupies the second constituent: a constituent can be a word or a whole phrase, not necessarily one written word. Der Mann ist hier means “The man is here”; Hier ist ein Zimmer means “Here is a room”. Der Mann is one constituent. In a yes/no question the finite verb comes first: Ist der Kolben sauber? (“Is the flask clean?”). A question word comes before the verb: Wo ist er? (“Where is he?”). Nicht negates: Er ist nicht groß (“He is not tall”). It does not move ist out of its normal position. Kein Geld (“no money”) and kein Mönch (“no monk”) are reading chunks here, not a new declension exercise.

The story also supplies a limited set of action forms for recognition: heißt (“is called”), wäscht (“washes”), trägt (“carries”), kommt (“comes”), zahlt (“pays”), sagt (“says”), fragt (“asks”), geht (“goes”), sieht (“sees”), hält (“holds”), weiß (“knows”). Weiß can also be the adjective “white”: Die Wäsche ist weiß (“The laundry is white”), but Jakob weiß es nicht (“Jakob does not know”). Sieht … an is “looks at”: Er sieht Jakob an (“He looks at Jakob”); the final an belongs with the verb. Geh means “Go!”; these action forms are not conjugation targets yet.

Read the exact location/ownership phrases as units for now: im Kloster (“in the monastery”), im Laboratorium (“in the laboratory”), in der Hauptstraße (“in the Hauptstraße”), von dem Mann (“belonging to the man”), von Herrn Weller (“belonging to Mr Weller”), für Herrn Weller (“for Mr Weller”), auf dem Tisch (“on the table”), in dem Kolben (“in the flask”), in das Licht (“into the light”), vor Jakob (“in front of Jakob”), bei Professor Bunsen (“at Professor Bunsen’s”), mit einer Zigarre (“with a cigar”), zu Hause (“at home”), am Wasser (“at the water”). The changed articles dem/den/einer and the form Herrn are case forms: German marks a noun phrase’s role. Their full patterns come later; do not infer a general rule from these chunks. Hände is the plural of Hand (“hands”); Studenten is plural “students”; one Woche (“week”), three Wochen (“weeks”).

Mein Vater means “my father”; meine Mutter means “my mother”; Ihr Problem means “your problem”, addressed respectfully to Bunsen. Man means people in general: Hier im Laboratorium ist man nicht laut (“One is not loud here in the laboratory”). Doch contradicts a negative: Das ist nicht mein Problem — Doch! (“That is not my problem — Yes, it is!”). Dreizehn Jahre alt means “thirteen years old”. Morgen is “tomorrow”, der Morgen “the morning”; sieben Uhr is “seven o’clock”.

Bunsen’s capitalised Er addresses Jakob directly: Wie heißt Er? literally has “he” grammar but means “What is your name?”; Ist Er stark? means “Are you strong?”. This is a deliberate nineteenth-century, socially unequal way of addressing a boy or servant, not modern polite German and not a third person standing nearby. It takes third-person singular forms. Jakob’s puzzled Er? is part of the scene. Jakob answers Herr Professor (“Professor”, respectfully). Do not copy this address in modern conversation; the course will move Bunsen to Sie later.
